diaphanous

dy-AF-uh-nus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Diaphanous is light, delicate, and translucent; sheer enough to see through.

Morning fog hung over the valley in diaphanous sheets that thinned as the sun rose higher.

Example

The dancer's diaphanous scarf floated behind her, so sheer that the stage lights shone straight through it.

A scarf so sheer that stage lights shine straight through it is exactly diaphanous.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sheer: Sheer describes fabric woven so fine and thin that you can see through it -- sheer curtains, sheer stockings. Diaphanous goes beyond that plain fact about thinness: it adds delicacy and airy lightness, and it can describe mist or light as well as cloth.

gauzy: Gauzy means thin and loose like gauze, full of tiny open gaps that light slips past. Diaphanous is broader: any fabric, mist, or light that is fine, airy, and see-through counts as diaphanous, whatever its texture happens to be.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

solid: not able to be seen through

Where it sits · how delicate and airy it is

thin → diaphanous → gossamer

thin vs. diaphanous: Thin describes any lack of thickness, in fabric or otherwise -- a plain, ordinary word; diaphanous specifically emphasizes delicate translucence, letting light pass through.

gossamer vs. diaphanous: Gossamer pushes delicacy to an almost otherworldly lightness, like a spider's web, while diaphanous is the more general word for anything sheer enough to see through.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — dia-: through (Greek)

root — phan: to show, appear (Greek (phainein))

suffix — -ous: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together: Diaphanous combines Greek dia- ('through') + phainein ('to show, appear') + -ous -- literally 'showing through.'

Use the root in a new word: phantom: The stagehands' nickname for the theater's ancient elevator is 'the phantom.'

Word Choice

Diaphanous is most often used for delicate fabrics, mist, or light, and can also describe anything non-literally thin or unconvincing, as in 'a diaphanous excuse.'
